04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

James's five-minute concession had already stretched beyond its promised limit. Emma was putting her notebook away when Nora interrupted the movement with a quiet request.

“There is something else, although I suspect it's the least reliable part.”

Emma stopped. “Then tell me the part you're confident about first.”

Nora described the vehicle as dark blue, with a shallow dent near its left rear light. She thought the streetlamp had caught the damaged metal as the car pulled away. Yet the precision of that image troubled her: she could picture the dent clearly without knowing whether it belonged to the car she had seen Claire enter.

“I'd noticed a similar car outside the community hall,” Nora explained. “More than once, I think. It may be that I'm carrying an image from one evening into another.”

Emma asked what connected the hall to the disappearance.

“Not what. Perhaps who. I once saw a man standing beside that other car after an event run by the education trust. I recognised him from the meetings.”

James's mug made a sharp sound against the table. “Mum, you don't owe her a name.”

Nora acknowledged him with a nod, then looked directly at Emma. “Reid. That is the surname I remember. I couldn't tell you what role he had, or even whether he owned the vehicle.”

Emma wrote the name followed by a question mark. Her first impulse was to ask whether Reid had helped Claire disappear. Instead she asked a narrower question: “Did you see him in the vehicle on the night Claire left?”

“No. I never saw the driver's face. I can't even establish that it was the same car.”

James folded his arms. “You know what a reporter can do with three things that nearly fit together.”

“Yes,” Emma said. She remembered the article she had written after Claire disappeared: a disputed personal account, insufficiently corroborated, had acquired the authority of print. She had learnt, too late, that cautious verbs in a paragraph did little to soften a damaging headline.

“I won't identify a driver on the strength of this conversation,” she said. “The name is a lead. The connection needs evidence.”

Nora searched a kitchen drawer and produced a photograph from a summer gathering. Her sister appeared among the people outside the hall. At the far edge of the image stood a dark car, cropped so tightly that its number plate was unreadable.

“That's why I've kept it,” Nora said, touching her sister's face in the picture. “Not because of the car. For all I know, it's entirely unrelated.”

Emma resisted the urge to photograph it immediately. She asked whether Nora might be willing to send a scan once she had considered the request. Nora made no promise beyond thinking about it.

At the door, James said, “Investigate whatever you need to. But don't give us another certainty that turns out to be somebody else's guess.”

In the rain, Emma separated what she had heard into three propositions: Nora recalled damage to a vehicle; she remembered a similar vehicle at the hall; and she associated a man called Reid with the latter occasion. None established ownership, presence on the night, or participation in Claire's departure.

She had obtained a possible route towards verification, not a conclusion. For once, that distinction felt more valuable than a headline.
